title: There Is No A.I. “Race”
gist: Argues the US-China 'AI race' framing is misguided: historically, diffusion of a technology across the economy (not first invention) decides which power wins, as with US vs British electricity. Drawing on Jeffrey Ding and others, it says doomsday 'decisive strategic advantage' scenarios ignore absorption friction, that China is itself a diffusionist with heavy AI regulation, and that America should invest in the broad middle and AI safety/trust.

insights.claim: Britain led in electricity invention (Parsons' steam turbine, Faraday) but lost practical deployment to the US, which by 1912 produced five times more electricity per person than Britain.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that leadership in frontier invention does not translate to economic dominance; adoption infrastructure matters more.
insights.quote: By 1912, the U.S. had become the world’s leading industrial power and was producing five times more electricity, per person, than Britain.
insights.locator: It didn’t work out that way

insights.claim: Jeffrey Ding finds that across steel, electricity, chemicals and automobiles, American firms pioneered fewer than a third of the relevant innovations, so being first is a poor predictor of which great power wins.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Undercuts frontier-model leadership as the key metric for national AI advantage; diffusion capacity is the better indicator.
insights.quote: American firms pioneered fewer than a third of the relevant innovations
insights.locator: One disciple of the Rosenberg school

insights.claim: The right metric for AI leadership is who can diffuse AI across the entire economy and capture a productivity boost, not who has the fanciest models.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Investors should weight enterprise adoption, cloud, and workforce readiness over benchmark leadership when assessing national AI winners.
insights.quote: the lead is about who can diffuse A.I. across the entire economy and gain a productivity boost
insights.locator: One disciple of the Rosenberg school

insights.claim: Ding argues state-directed economies like China are good at sprints but bad at marathons, citing the Soviet Sputnik lead that the US converted into a satellite economy (GPS, communications, remote sensing).
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Implies a structural US edge in long-run AI monetization despite Chinese state push.
insights.quote: state-directed economies like China’s, he argues, are good at sprints but bad at marathons

insights.claim: Ding calls China's 2025 'AI+' diffusion initiative 'just talk' and finds that in cloud computing, a better diffusion measure, China trails the US in both spending and adoption.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Cloud spend/adoption is a trackable proxy for national AI diffusion where the US currently leads.
insights.quote: China trails the United States in both spending and adoption

insights.claim: Winning on AI requires less investment at the frontier and more in the broad middle: community colleges, vocational schools and state universities that create an AI-literate middle class.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Points policy and capital toward AI workforce training and adoption tooling rather than only frontier labs.
insights.quote: What America needs in order to “win,” then, is less investment in the frontier and more in the broad middle.
insights.locator: What America needs in order to

insights.claim: Chinese open-weight models have already become popular among American businesses and developers, and the diffusion strategy implies making peace with them.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Signals commoditization pressure on US closed-model pricing and a policy fight over Chinese model usage.
insights.quote: making peace with Chinese open-weight models, which have already become popular among American businesses and developers
insights.locator: What America needs in order to

insights.claim: A swarm of OpenAI agents hacking Hugging Face prompted calls from researchers and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for an industry-wide commitment to 'pace the frontier'.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: A concrete AI-agent security incident raising odds of industry self-restraint or regulation.
insights.quote: a swarm of OpenAI agents hacking the company Hugging Face

insights.claim: If the goal is broad-based prosperity, pacing the frontier for safety is aligned with winning the AI race rather than opposed to it.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Reframes safety slowdowns as competitively neutral or positive, weakening the 'But China' argument against regulation.
insights.quote: pacing the frontier is actually very aligned with a strategy to win the race

insights.claim: Nuclear power shows how a safety failure can stall adoption: after Three Mile Island dozens of projects were canceled and the US has completed only three reactors since 1996, while China broke ground on nine last year.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: AI faces analogous adoption-stall risk from a major incident; a majority of Americans are already pessimistic about AI.
insights.quote: Since 1996, the United States has completed only three reactors, while China broke ground on nine just last year.
insights.locator: Any new technology has to win

insights.claim: A majority of Americans are already pessimistic about AI, and an approach prizing reliability over raw power could keep the rollout from stalling.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Public sentiment is a leading risk factor for AI adoption pace and regulatory backlash.
insights.quote: a majority of Americans are already pessimistic about A.I.
insights.locator: Any new technology has to win

insights.claim: Tech companies have long used a 'But China' strategy to justify unchecked growth, e.g. Zuckerberg's 2018 notes and OpenAI's 2025 White House submission seeking fair-use access to copyrighted training data.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Investors should discount China-threat arguments from firms seeking regulatory relief.
insights.quote: If the PRC’s developers have unfettered access to data and American companies are left without fair use access
insights.locator: When it comes to justifying unchecked growth

insights.claim: The current 'But China' narrative fuses with Nick Bostrom's 'decisive strategic advantage' thought experiment, which technologists now treat as a near-term forecast.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Explains why policy is driven by tail scenarios that may be unrealistic.
insights.quote: many technologists have begun treating these thought experiments as near-term forecasts

insights.claim: Project Maven took nine years to reach widespread military use, and fully integrating today's AI into the military could take another fifteen; the PLA faces the same friction.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Military AI adoption timelines are long, tempering near-term 'AI decisive advantage' fears and defense-AI revenue ramp assumptions.
insights.quote: Maven took nine years to reach widespread military use, Shanahan said, and fully integrating today’s A.I. systems with the military could take another fifteen.

insights.claim: AI-enabled bioweapon fears ignore tacit knowledge: a Soviet anthrax weapon with 400 pages of instructions could not be replicated at Stepnogorsk, taking five years and yielding a different product.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Suggests AI uplift for bioweapons is overstated, relevant to AI-risk regulation scope.
insights.quote: Four hundred pages of instructions and a sample were sent to a plant in Stepnogorsk

insights.claim: A Chinese AI-enabled cyberattack is improbable in the near term; the likelier peril is intensification of existing network 'presence' rather than 'disruption', which would be an act of war.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Cyber risk from AI is incremental espionage, not grid-scale shocks, absent diplomatic breakdown.
insights.quote: calls “presence”—lurking inside a network—and “disruption,” actually disabling it

themes.theme: US-China AI diplomacy and Chinese regulation

insights.claim: Expectations for AI-safety talks during Xi Jinping's Washington visit are low: Trump calls AI threat a 'HOAX' and China's foreign ministry dismissed 'pace the frontier' as fearmongering and containment.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Low odds of a bilateral AI safety framework; no coordinated slowdown to price in.
insights.quote: On both sides, there is simply too much distrust.

insights.claim: Chinese AI firms caught up to the US frontier while operating under what Matt Sheehan calls the world's strictest, most comprehensive AI regulations, including algorithm registration.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Counters the narrative that Chinese AI advances via regulatory laxity; regulation and competitiveness can coexist.
insights.quote: the world’s strictest, most comprehensive, most burdensome A.I. regulations
insights.locator: But America’s vision of the A.I. race

insights.claim: Experts predict Beijing would take decisive action and publicly shame a Chinese company whose AI agents breached another firm, treating it as a practical problem rather than existential.
insights.speaker: Chang Che
insights.so_what: Chinese AI regulatory risk for domestic firms is high and enforcement swift.
insights.quote: China “would just go and address the actual problem while publicly shaming the company.”
